opening: Poland says all three objects that fell on its soil were Russian cruise missiles, as NATO allies meet. Ukraine says it sank a Russian warship in Libya, Trump threatened new strikes on Iran after the new year, and the AI share sell-off spread across Asia.

stories.title: Polish prosecutors say all three objects that came down in Poland were Russian cruise missiles, as NATO allies meet on Monday
stories.body: Polish prosecutors said on Sunday that all three objects that fell in eastern Poland on Friday were Russian Kh-101 cruise missiles, including one the defence minister had first described as a probable jet drone. Preliminary findings say the missiles were built this autumn at a Russian plant in Dubna. They spent about three minutes in Polish airspace; two Swedish Gripen jets on NATO patrol could not identify them in bad weather. The North Atlantic Council meets in Brussels on Monday to discuss the incursion.
stories.whatChanged: Poland now has a formal finding that every object was a Russian cruise missile, which it will bring to the emergency NATO meeting on Monday.
stories.whyMatters: A confirmed Russian missile incursion into a NATO member puts pressure on the alliance to show it can detect and stop such weapons, and tests how far allies will go to reinforce the eastern flank.
stories.uncertainty: Russia had not commented on Poland’s findings in the reports we read. It is not known why the missiles crossed into Poland, and no new allied deployments had been announced before the meeting.
stories.watchNext: What Mark Rutte announces after the North Atlantic Council session, and whether allies answer Poland’s requests for more surveillance aircraft and fighter jets.
keyFacts: Prosecutors in Lublin identified all three objects as Kh-101 cruise missiles on Sunday, November 22
The missiles were in Polish airspace for about three minutes, a Polish military commander said
Two Swedish Gripen jets on NATO air policing could not identify the targets in bad weather
One missile fell about 22 miles from Nowa Dęba, where allied troops were exercising
Nobody was hurt and no damage was reported

report.heading: What the investigation found
paragraphs: The district prosecutor’s office in Lublin, working with military prosecutors and the Military Gendarmerie, said on Sunday that the three objects that crashed near Nowy Lipowiec, Rudnik nad Sanem and Mołodycz on Friday were all Kh-101 cruise missiles. Earlier the defence ministry had suggested one of them was probably a jet-powered drone. According to the preliminary findings, the missiles were made in the final quarter of 2026 in Dubna, near Moscow, where the manufacturer MKB Raduga is based.

Justice Minister Waldemar Żurek said the evidence put an end to false claims about what had happened. The objects were over Poland for roughly three minutes, according to operational commander Ireneusz Nowak. Two Swedish Gripens flying NATO air policing missions tried to intercept them but could not identify them in poor weather; Kyiv Post reported that one pilot had been cleared to fire but held off.

report.heading: What Poland wants from NATO
paragraphs: In Warsaw on Saturday, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said the alliance would defend every inch of Polish territory and that its top commander, US General Alexus Grynkewich, was reviewing allied defences for weaknesses. He did not rule out a repeat.

Poland is sending Deputy Defence Minister Paweł Zalewski to Monday’s session. According to UNN, Warsaw wants its own account of the incident heard, a clear show of allied solidarity and concrete proposals to strengthen air defence on the eastern flank. It does not currently plan to invoke Article 4 or expect a joint statement. Poland has asked for more NATO surveillance aircraft and F-35 fighters. Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said it was hard to see the incident as a coincidence, because one missile landed about 22 miles from a site where allied troops were training.

report.heading: What is still missing
paragraphs: Moscow had not responded to the Polish findings in the reports we read. No outcome of the North Atlantic Council meeting was available at our cutoff, and no new deployments to Poland had been announced.

stories.title: Ukraine says its sea drones sank a Russian warship docked in Libya, its first acknowledged attack in the Mediterranean
stories.body: President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Monday that seven Ukrainian naval drones sank the Russian corvette Merkury at the naval base in Benghazi, eastern Libya, on Sunday. He said the attack also destroyed a Russian navy helicopter and hit a cargo ship that he says was carrying Russian weapons. Libyan officials said the warship was badly damaged and capsized, and that it had stopped to refuel under an agreement with Russia. No casualties were reported, and Moscow had not commented.
stories.whatChanged: Ukraine has struck a Russian warship far from the Black Sea for the first time it has acknowledged, two days after drones hit a Russian military cargo ship in the Baltic.
stories.whyMatters: The attack shows Kyiv can reach Russian naval assets across the Mediterranean, and it pulls Libya, divided between rival governments, further into the war.
stories.uncertainty: Accounts differ: Libyan officials told the Associated Press that four drones were shot down and two hit the ship, while Kyiv says seven were used and the ship sank. Russia has not confirmed any loss, and how the drones reached Libya is unclear.
stories.watchNext: Whether Russia confirms the loss or retaliates, and what the joint Libyan–Russian investigation and any United Nations inquiry find.
keyFacts: The corvette Merkury entered service in 2023 and was docked at Benghazi naval base
Zelensky says seven Ukrainian-made naval drones were used
Ukraine also claims a Ka-27 helicopter destroyed and the cargo ship Angara hit
Libyan officials told AP at least four drones were intercepted and two struck the ship
No casualties were reported

report.heading: What happened
paragraphs: Several explosions hit the Merkury, a Russian corvette commissioned in 2023, while it was moored at the naval base in Benghazi on Sunday, and the ship capsized. On Monday Zelensky called it an exemplary Ukrainian operation and said seven Ukrainian-built sea drones had been used. He said a Russian Ka-27 helicopter was destroyed and that the cargo ship Angara, which he accused of carrying Russian weapons, was also hit. Ukraine’s Security Service released video and said the drones had been launched from a mother ship; a joint statement said Russia had no safe routes.
It is the first operation of its kind that Kyiv has acknowledged in Libya, and it came a day after drones set the Russian military cargo ship Sparta II on fire in the Gulf of Finland.

report.heading: Libya’s response
paragraphs: The eastern administration aligned with Khalifa Haftar said the warship had put in to refuel under a cooperation agreement with Moscow, and opened a joint investigation with Russia. Libyan officials told the Associated Press that at least four drones were intercepted and two struck the vessel, figures that differ from Zelensky’s account. Eastern Libya’s prime minister, Osama Hamad, asked the United Nations to investigate a suspected launch from western Libya.
The internationally recognised government in Tripoli condemned the use of Libyan territory for a proxy conflict. The Russian defence ministry had not commented at our cutoff.

report.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: Russia has used eastern Libya as a foothold in the Mediterranean and Africa. A Ukrainian strike there shows how far Kyiv’s long-range maritime drone campaign now extends, and risks entangling a country that remains split between rival authorities.

stories.title: Trump says he is inclined to resume major strikes on Iran after the new year, and Tehran vows to use every means against the blockade
stories.region: Middle East · Iran and the Gulf
stories.body: President Trump told Fox News on Sunday that he was inclined to order major new strikes on Iran after the new year if there is no deal, called Iran’s negotiators professional tap dancers, and said any ships that try to run the US naval blockade would end up at the bottom of the sea. On Monday Iran’s foreign ministry called the blockade military aggression and said Tehran would use every means against it. The British maritime agency reported another incident involving a tanker in the Gulf of Oman on Sunday.
stories.whatChanged: Washington has set out a rough timetable for renewed strikes, and Tehran has answered with a pledge to fight the blockade, even as Qatar tries to mediate.
stories.whyMatters: A return to full-scale strikes would end the uneasy pause in the war and deepen the shipping crisis in and around the Strait of Hormuz, through which much of the world’s oil normally passes.
stories.uncertainty: Trump has not said what would count as a deal. Iranian media say tanker convoys to test the blockade are being planned, but no official body has announced one, and details of Sunday’s incident in the Gulf of Oman have not been released.
stories.watchNext: Talks between Qatar’s prime minister and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, which Euronews reported were expected on Monday, and whether any Iranian tanker convoy sails.
keyFacts: Trump said on November 22 that he was inclined to resume major strikes after the new year if no deal is reached
Iran’s foreign ministry spokesman called the blockade an act of military aggression on November 23
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Hormuz could reopen within two hours once Iran’s conditions are met
US Central Command marked 130 days of the renewed blockade on November 21
Iran’s power authority said rolling blackouts would begin on November 22 because of fuel shortages

report.heading: Washington’s warning
paragraphs: In an interview with Fox News broadcast on Sunday, Trump said that without an agreement he was leaning towards renewing large-scale strikes on Iran after the new year. He described Iran’s negotiators as professional tap dancers and said they had become more aggressive than before the election. Asked about Iranian ships testing the blockade, he said he hoped they would try, because they would be sunk like the rest of Iran’s navy.
The US Central Command marked 130 days of the renewed blockade on Saturday, and earlier in the week the United States extended it to vessels taking Iranian cargo in transfers at sea.

report.heading: Tehran’s answer
paragraphs: At his weekly briefing on Monday, foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei called the blockade military aggression and a crime, and said Iran would use every means to counter it. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said the Strait of Hormuz could reopen within two hours once the other side met its commitments, which Iran defines as lifting sanctions, ending the blockade and implementing a memorandum agreed in Islamabad that Trump has called void.

Iran’s Tasnim news agency said plans for tanker convoys were being drawn up, but no convoy has been ordered. The UK Maritime Trade Operations centre confirmed an incident involving a tanker and military forces in the Gulf of Oman on Sunday without giving details.

report.heading: Mediation and pressure at home
paragraphs: A Qatari delegation held about two hours of talks in Tehran on Friday evening, according to Iran’s deputy foreign minister, who said enriched uranium would not leave the country. Inside Iran, the head of the power utility said rolling blackouts would start on Sunday because of fuel supply problems, and President Masoud Pezeshkian warned of a hard winter.

stories.title: The AI share sell-off spreads through Asia, triggering a trading halt in Seoul and a short-selling ban in Taiwan
stories.body: Asian markets kept falling on Monday after Wall Street’s worst week since April 2025. South Korea’s main index, the Kospi, fell as much as 5.8 per cent and briefly halted program trading; it is now nearly half below its June record. Taiwan’s regulator banned short selling below the previous day’s close from Monday, after the island’s main index lost more than six per cent on Friday. Australian shares fell for an eighth straight session, while US stock futures pointed to a rebound.
stories.whatChanged: The sell-off in AI-linked shares, which pushed US indexes into a correction last week, has turned into emergency market measures in Asia’s chipmaking economies.
stories.whyMatters: South Korea and Taiwan are home to the chipmakers at the centre of the AI boom, so steep falls there hit savers and pension funds directly and show how concentrated the global market has become in a single theme.
stories.uncertainty: It is not clear whether Sunday night’s rebound in US futures will hold when New York opens, or whether Taiwan’s short-selling ban and Korea’s calls for a stabilisation fund will slow the falls.
stories.watchNext: How Wall Street trades in a holiday-shortened week, with markets closed on Thursday for Thanksgiving, and the Federal Reserve’s decision on December 9.
keyFacts: The S&P 500 fell 3.7 per cent on Friday, November 20, and 8.4 per cent over the week
Taiwan’s main index lost 6.23 per cent on Friday and is about 28 per cent below its October record
Taiwan’s ban on short selling below the previous close took effect on Monday, November 23
Seoul’s Kospi fell as much as 5.8 per cent on Monday before trimming losses
Australia’s ASX 200 fell for an eighth straight session on Monday

report.heading: Asia’s Monday
paragraphs: In Seoul, the Kospi fell as much as 5.8 per cent on Monday, and a five-minute pause in sell-side program trading kicked in late in the morning. By mid-afternoon the index was down about 3.2 per cent, at roughly 48 per cent below its June record, after a fall of more than five per cent on Friday. Retail investors were urging the government to activate a 100 trillion won stabilisation fund.
In Sydney, the ASX 200 slipped 0.3 per cent, its eighth consecutive decline, after its worst week since mid-2022.

report.heading: Taiwan steps in
paragraphs: Taiwan’s main index fell 6.23 per cent on Friday, one of its largest one-day point losses on record, leaving it about 28 per cent below its October 6 peak. On Saturday the Financial Supervisory Commission banned short selling below the previous close from Monday, the first blanket restriction of this kind since 2015, according to the Central News Agency. It also raised margin requirements for short sales, suspended new put warrants and encouraged listed companies to buy back shares. A national stabilisation fund of 500 billion Taiwan dollars has been authorised to buy shares since November 6.

report.heading: Wall Street’s week
paragraphs: The S&P 500 closed Friday at 6,910 after a seventh straight daily loss, and the Nasdaq has given up its gains for the year. Futures markets nonetheless put the chance of another Federal Reserve rate rise in December at about 92 per cent. On Sunday night, futures on the Dow Jones index were up about 800 points and Nasdaq futures nearly three per cent, Fortune reported, a rebound that would need to survive the New York open.

stories.title: Bangladesh says it will arrest Sheikh Hasina the moment she returns, after more than a week of violent unrest by her supporters
stories.body: Bangladesh’s government said on Monday that former prime minister Sheikh Hasina would be arrested as soon as she tries to enter the country, and that it wants India to extradite her instead. Hasina, who fled to India in 2024 and has been sentenced to death in her absence, plans to return in December. Her banned Awami League has staged protests since November 14, and local media have counted dozens of crude bomb blasts and vehicle arsons in at least 28 districts over ten days.
stories.whatChanged: The government has publicly committed to arresting Hasina on arrival, turning her planned return into a direct confrontation.
stories.whyMatters: A return by Hasina could bring her supporters and the new government into open conflict, and the dispute strains relations with India, which is sheltering her.
stories.uncertainty: Hasina has given no date for her return, the government has refused her a new passport, and it is not clear who is behind the attacks; the prime minister has blamed India, which did not respond to Reuters.
stories.watchNext: Whether Hasina names a date for her return in December, and how India answers Bangladesh’s request for extradition.
keyFacts: A state minister for foreign affairs said Hasina would be arrested as soon as she tries to enter Bangladesh
Hasina was sentenced to death in absentia and the Awami League is banned
At least four people have been killed since protests began on November 14, Al Jazeera reports
22 branches of Grameen Bank were among the targets of attacks
Bangladesh deployed 90 more platoons of border guards

report.heading: The government’s warning
paragraphs: A state minister for foreign affairs told Reuters on Monday that Hasina would be detained as soon as she tried to come back, and that Dhaka wanted India to hand her over under the two countries’ extradition treaty. Hasina has said she intends to return in December but has not given a date. The government rejected her application for a new passport and identity card earlier this month.
She has been sentenced to death in her absence, and her party, the Awami League, is banned from politics.

report.heading: A week of violence
paragraphs: Supporters of the former prime minister have held protests since November 14, including a nationwide lockdown called for November 19. Bangladeshi media counted dozens of crude bomb explosions and vehicle arsons across at least 28 districts. Al Jazeera reports at least four deaths, three political activists and a bus worker. Attackers targeted police stations and banks, including 22 branches of Grameen Bank, and set fire to the ancestral home of Muhammad Yunus in Chittagong; nobody was hurt there and the arsonists have not been identified.

The government sent 90 additional platoons of the Border Guard Bangladesh onto the streets. Prime Minister Tarique Rahman told parliament on Friday that India was to blame. India’s foreign ministry did not respond to Reuters’ request for comment.

report.heading: Context
paragraphs: Hasina fled to India in 2024 after mass protests ended her long rule. Her planned return has become the main source of tension in Bangladeshi politics since the new government took office.

stories.title: Russia tows the drone-hit cargo ship Sparta II out of Finnish waters, and the Kremlin accuses Ukraine of terrorism in the Baltic
stories.whatChanged: The burning ship has left Finnish waters under Russian tow, and Moscow has blamed Kyiv for the attack.
stories.body: After two days of firefighting, a Russian rescue vessel began towing the sanctioned military cargo ship Sparta II out of Finnish waters on Sunday; Finland’s border guard said some containers were still warm but no fire was visible and nothing was leaking. On Monday Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov spoke of a dangerous trend of terrorist activity by Ukraine in the Baltic. Finnish officials have said Ukraine was likely responsible; Kyiv has not claimed the attack.

stories.title: The death toll in the drone strike on an apartment block in Dymer, near Kyiv, rises to 11
stories.whatChanged: Rescuers have recovered more bodies from the partly collapsed building, and the Kyiv region held a day of mourning on Monday.
stories.body: The head of the Kyiv regional administration said on Monday that 11 people were now known to have died after a Russian drone partly brought down a five-storey building in Dymer; a seven-year-old boy was pulled out alive after about 14 hours. A drone also hit a supermarket in Vyshneve on Sunday evening, killing at least two people. Overnight, Ukraine’s air force said Russia launched 153 drones and that 134 were shot down or jammed.

stories.title: After COP31’s collapse, the UN chief blames fossil fuel interests and Australia’s opposition calls on Chris Bowen to resign
stories.whatChanged: The fallout from the failed Antalya summit has begun, with blame directed at oil-producing states and political pressure on the Australian minister who led the negotiations.
stories.body: UN Secretary-General António Guterres said he was deeply disappointed that COP31 ended without consensus and blamed powerful fossil fuel interests; the EU’s climate commissioner, Wopke Hoekstra, said the final text failed even to acknowledge the need to move away from fossil fuels. Russia’s negotiator said Moscow could not accept any such wording. In Canberra on Monday, opposition leader Angus Taylor called on Chris Bowen, who presided over the negotiations, to resign. Pacific states including the Marshall Islands and Vanuatu condemned the outcome.

stories.title: Drone strikes hit homes and a UN building in Sudan’s capital, and the army accuses Ethiopia
stories.whatChanged: The war’s drone campaign has reached Khartoum again, damaging United Nations premises with staff inside.
stories.body: Explosions were heard near Khartoum airport and elsewhere in the city early on Sunday, destroying at least one house, and the UN humanitarian office said a UN building with staff inside was damaged. An army source told AFP the drones were launched from Ethiopia, which denies helping the Rapid Support Forces. Casualty reports differ: AFP said none were immediately reported, while Australia’s ABC cited local reports of at least four civilians killed.

stories.title: Police remove 24 body bags from a fire-gutted sweet factory in Indonesia, with dozens of workers still missing
stories.whatChanged: Search teams have recovered remains from the factory, but the death toll is still unclear.
stories.body: Fire swept through a three-storey confectionery factory in Cikande, in Indonesia’s Banten province, on Saturday afternoon. Police have removed 24 body bags, but say the toll is not yet known because some may hold remains of more than one person, and DNA identification could take weeks. Counts of the missing differ between the company and the authorities, and parts of the building are at risk of collapse. The cause is under investigation.

stories.whatChanged: The first enforcement step after the World Court’s genocide ruling: France wants the Security Council to take up Myanmar’s refusal to comply.
stories.body: France’s foreign ministry said on Saturday that it would seek a Security Council meeting after Myanmar’s military-backed government rejected last week’s ruling by the International Court of Justice that it committed genocide against the Rohingya. Paris said the court’s rulings are final and binding, and noted that the UN Charter lets the Council act when a party does not comply. About 1.2 million Rohingya refugees live in Bangladesh.

stories.whatChanged: The confrontation between President Abelardo de la Espriella and his predecessor has moved onto social media and into a dispute over censorship.
stories.body: Gustavo Petro posted a speech on Saturday urging Colombians to demand President De la Espriella’s resignation, repeating allegations of electoral fraud that election observers reject. stories.title: As mathematicians check the AI-assisted Riemann proof, a separate 940-page human-written proof is posted for review
stories.body: Mathematicians are still testing Levent Alpöge’s claim that he and Claude, Anthropic’s AI system, proved the Riemann Hypothesis in some 17 million lines of Lean code. The code compiled at MIT and Carnegie Mellon, but slower checks for hidden shortcuts in how the theorem was stated were still running in the latest reporting we read. Meanwhile, the president of the American Mathematical Society posted a 940-page, entirely human manuscript by Alessandro Masullo that also claims a proof. Specialists remain cautious about both.
stories.whatChanged: The AI-assisted claim now has a rival human-written one, and reporting makes clear that the decisive formal checks were not finished when the first claims of success circulated.
stories.whyMatters: A proof would settle one of mathematics’ central open questions. How the two claims are checked, one readable by people and one readable only by machines, will shape how mathematicians treat AI-produced results.
stories.hook: Two very different claimed proofs of a 167-year-old problem are now under scrutiny; neither has yet been accepted, and the machine checks on the AI-assisted one were still under way.
stories.uncertainty: We could not confirm the report, which we repeated on Sunday, that the Lean community had endorsed the AI-assisted proof; the checks that would test for that were still running in the latest account we read. The human manuscript is a draft, and an earlier attempt by the same author did not hold up.
stories.watchNext: Results of the comparator checks on the Lean code, and whether number theorists begin a formal review of either proof.
keyFacts: Alpöge posted a four-page paper on November 20 and says he reached the result on November 16
Producing readable text from Claude ran to more than 250,000 pages, so he released Lean code instead
Andrew Sutherland at MIT and Simon DeDeo at Carnegie Mellon compiled the code independently
Ravi Vakil, president of the American Mathematical Society, posted Masullo’s 940-page manuscript
Vakil said Brian Conrad had reviewed the human manuscript for months

report.heading: Where the AI-assisted claim stands
paragraphs: Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, said in a four-page paper posted on November 20 that he and Claude had found a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, and that the code also verifies the stronger generalised version. There is no human-readable proof: asking Claude for one produced more than 250,000 pages, so he released about 17 million lines of Lean, a language in which a computer checks every step.

Andrew Sutherland at MIT compiled the code first, and Simon DeDeo at Carnegie Mellon did so a few hours later. Compiling is not the last word. Further comparator checks, which look for definitions quietly altered to make a statement trivially true, cannot be split across machines and were expected to take hours or days. Quanta reported no results from them.

report.heading: Reactions
paragraphs: DeDeo said he would be very surprised to find any hidden tricks, and Filippo Nuccio of Jean Monnet University praised the scope of the formal work. Maksym Radziwiłł of New York University was critical, arguing that a proof made of machine code bypasses understanding and does not explain why the result is true. Many number theorists are withholding judgement.

report.heading: A human proof appears
paragraphs: Separately, Ravi Vakil of Stanford, president of the American Mathematical Society, posted a 940-page manuscript by Alessandro Masullo that claims a proof of the generalised hypothesis, written without AI. Vakil said Brian Conrad had been reviewing it for months. Number theorists are wary because an earlier attempt by the same author did not survive scrutiny, and members of the Lean community have begun discussing whether to formalise it.
The Signal is produced with the help of Claude, the AI system involved in the first claim.

stories.title: UN talks on AI-run weapons end with a two-year mandate to work on rules, but no move to negotiate a binding treaty
stories.body: The 128 countries that belong to the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons agreed in Geneva on Saturday to elaborate a possible agreement on lethal autonomous weapons over the next two years, aiming at 2028. Nearly 100 states had pushed for swift negotiations on legally binding rules, but the United States, Russia and Israel opposed them, and the convention works by consensus. Some countries refused even the word negotiate. Campaigners called the mandate watered down.
stories.whatChanged: The review conference has ended with a mandate to keep working rather than to negotiate a treaty, pushing any binding rules on autonomous weapons to 2028 at the earliest.
stories.whyMatters: AI-guided weapons are already being used in current wars, and this forum is the main place where nearly all military powers discuss limits on them.
stories.hook: A modest procedural step: talks continue, but the main military powers blocked a push for binding rules on weapons that select targets without a human decision.
stories.uncertainty: The text of the mandate and how much it binds states to produce were not detailed in the reports we read, and it is unclear whether frustrated countries will pursue a treaty outside the convention.
stories.watchNext: Whether the nearly 100 states that wanted negotiations start a separate treaty process, as campaigners propose.
keyFacts: 128 states agreed on Saturday, November 21, to elaborate a possible accord over two years
Nearly 100 countries backed swift negotiation of legally binding rules
The United States, Russia and Israel opposed that push
UN Secretary-General António Guterres had called for clear prohibitions and restrictions
Decisions under the convention require consensus

report.heading: What was agreed
paragraphs: The seventh review conference of the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons closed in Geneva on Saturday after talks on the final wording ran through the night. Its member states agreed to elaborate on a possible accord covering lethal autonomous weapons over the next two years. The Swiss diplomat chairing the conference said some countries had rejected the word negotiate, but called the result a significant step for humanitarian disarmament.

Nearly 100 countries had wanted to move quickly to legally binding rules. The United States, Russia and Israel opposed this, and because the convention decides by consensus, any one state can block a decision. Russian procedural objections forced some formal sessions to be cancelled.

report.heading: Reaction
paragraphs: Stop Killer Robots, a coalition of about 300 organisations, called the mandate watered down; its executive director, Nicole van Rooijen, said delay puts civilians at risk. Human Rights Watch called the outcome disappointing and said the technology is racing ahead.

When the conference opened on November 16, Guterres had urged delegates to agree a legally binding instrument with clear prohibitions and restrictions, and the UN human rights chief, Volker Türk, called for a ban on weapons that target people.

report.heading: Background
paragraphs: An expert group had already weakened its draft in September, removing prohibitions and replacing a reference to human control with softer language, Justice Info reported. In October, 163 states voted at the UN General Assembly to press ahead with the issue, and campaigners point to the treaties on landmines and cluster munitions, negotiated outside this forum, as a model.

stories.title: Fighting near an Ebola hospital in eastern Congo traps health workers for more than a day, as the country’s worst outbreak continues
stories.body: Health workers sheltered in a hospital maternity ward in Congo’s Ituri province for more than 24 hours as fighting raged nearby, the head of the World Health Organization said on Sunday, adding that the best medicine is peace. The WHO is arranging a safe exit for the team. The outbreak, Congo’s largest and deadliest, had caused 5,678 deaths among 11,613 cases by November 17. The WHO says transmission remains high, although some areas show a slight decline.
stories.whatChanged: Conflict is now directly endangering the people fighting the outbreak, with a medical team pinned down by fighting in one of the worst-hit provinces.
stories.whyMatters: Ebola is controlled by tracing contacts, isolating patients and vaccinating, all of which depend on health workers being able to move safely; fighting makes each of those harder.
stories.uncertainty: The report we read does not say who was fighting near the hospital or whether anyone was hurt, and WHO case figures lag by several days.
stories.watchNext: Whether the WHO team is evacuated safely, and the next WHO update on case numbers in Ituri and North Kivu.
keyFacts: Health workers sheltered for more than 24 hours in a hospital maternity ward in Ituri
WHO counted 5,678 deaths and 11,613 cases as of November 17
It is the largest and deadliest Ebola outbreak in Congo’s history
Ituri and North Kivu are the worst-affected provinces

report.heading: What happened
paragraphs: WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said on Sunday that heavy fighting near a hospital in Ituri had put patients and staff at grave risk. Health workers and partners took shelter in the maternity ward for more than a day, and the WHO said it was working to get the team out safely. Tedros said the best medicine is peace.

report.heading: The state of the outbreak
paragraphs: As of November 17 the WHO had recorded 11,613 cases and 5,678 deaths, making this Congo’s largest and deadliest Ebola outbreak. Ituri and North Kivu in the east are worst affected. A WHO statement on November 22 said some areas were showing a slight decline in new cases, but that transmission remains high overall.

report.heading: Why the fighting matters
paragraphs: Clashes between Congo’s army and the Rwanda-backed M23 rebels have disrupted deliveries of supplies, and earlier this month a group linked to the Islamic State raided villages in North Kivu, Al Jazeera reports. Every part of the response, from tracing the contacts of patients to running treatment centres, depends on medical teams being able to work in the affected areas.

On the same day, the presidents of Kenya and Congo, meeting in Oyo in the Republic of Congo to restore diplomatic ties, pledged to work together on preventing Ebola, according to China’s Xinhua news agency.

north-america.summary: Wall Street heads into Thanksgiving week after its worst week since April 2025, storms threaten holiday travel on both coasts, and Democrats push back against a new limit on what contractors can tell Congress.

briefs.title: Storms on both coasts threaten Thanksgiving travel
briefs.text: AccuWeather expects a storm to form over the Gulf on Tuesday and spread rain, coastal flooding and possible power cuts from the Southeast to the Northeast and Midwest by Thanksgiving, with airport delays likely from Florida to Boston and Detroit. In the West, Fox Weather forecasts back-to-back Pacific storms from Tuesday bringing several feet of snow to the Sierra, Cascades and Rockies and a higher flood risk in California. Forecasters say details may change because the eastern storm had not yet formed.

briefs.title: Democrats vow to fight Trump’s order on contractors and Congress
briefs.text: President Trump’s order requiring federal contractors to consult the White House before answering congressional inquiries drew sharp criticism over the weekend. Representative Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the Oversight Committee, called it a blatant attack on Congress’s power of oversight, and Democrats sent letters asking a dozen current and former officials to preserve records. No legal challenge had been filed in the reports we read.

latin-america.summary: Troops remain in Sinaloa after the capture of a most-wanted cartel leader, Brazil’s jailed former president is in intensive care, and Colombia’s government is in a social media fight with its predecessor.

briefs.title: Mexican troops stay in Sinaloa after the capture of ‘El Chapo Isidro’
briefs.text: Mexico’s security secretary, Omar García Harfuch, said troops would remain deployed in Sinaloa after the operation that captured Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, in which four soldiers and seven alleged gunmen died. Meza Flores and two lieutenants were flown to Mexico City and handed to organised crime prosecutors, and US officials credited intelligence sharing. A tense calm has settled over Guasave, and no US extradition request had been reported.

briefs.title: Bolsonaro is in intensive care with a bowel obstruction
briefs.text: Brazil’s former president Jair Bolsonaro, 71, was admitted to a hospital in Brasília on Friday with a bowel obstruction and was described on Saturday as clinically stable and conscious, with no date for discharge. He is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup and has been under house arrest since March. His son Carlos said he might need another operation.

europe.summary: Poland takes its finding that Russian cruise missiles crossed its territory to NATO, Russia tows its drone-hit ship home from Finland, and Spain enters the last week before its snap election.

briefs.title: Spain’s right keeps its lead a week before the snap election
briefs.text: Most polls published before Spain’s November 29 election show the conservative People’s Party and the far-right Vox together above the 176 seats needed for a majority, though one pollster has the Socialists first and the right three seats short. Spain bans the publication of polls in the final five days of the campaign, starting on Tuesday, November 24. The only head-to-head debate between Pedro Sánchez and Alberto Núñez Feijóo, on November 19, drew more than ten million viewers.

briefs.title: EU leaders clash over a proposed cut to the next long-term budget
briefs.text: France called European Council President António Costa’s proposal for the 2028 to 2034 budget, which trims about ten per cent from the Commission’s draft, very disappointing and not a basis for agreement, especially on farm spending. Germany’s Friedrich Merz said the total was still too high, and Sweden said the 27 members were very far from a compromise. The Kyiv Independent reported that an internal Commission estimate puts interest on loans to Ukraine at 55.4 billion euros over the period.

briefs.title: A boat carrying mourners capsizes in Nigeria’s Bayelsa state
briefs.text: A boat taking people to a funeral overturned at a river junction in the Southern Ijaw area, and the National Emergency Management Agency said 24 bodies had been recovered. Police said 24 people were rescued. Residents told Reuters there were at least 300 people on board, a figure police did not confirm; overcrowding and mechanical failure have been cited, and the boat’s manager is in custody.

briefs.title: Kenya and Congo agree to restore full diplomatic relations
briefs.text: Presidents William Ruto and Félix Tshisekedi agreed at a meeting in Oyo, in the Republic of Congo, on Sunday to return their ambassadors and revive a joint cooperation commission, according to China’s Xinhua news agency. Relations had been strained since December 2023, when a rebel alliance that includes M23 was launched in Nairobi. The two leaders also pledged to work together against Ebola.

briefs.title: Saudi-led coalition intercepts a Houthi missile aimed at western Saudi Arabia
briefs.text: The Saudi-led coalition said on Sunday it had intercepted a ballistic missile fired by the Houthis towards the kingdom’s western region, which is home to the Yanbu South oil terminal and the Jazan refinery. It is the latest in a series of Houthi attacks on Saudi territory this month.

briefs.title: Israeli investigators find no evidence the election result was skewed
briefs.text: Police and Shin Bet investigators told the chair of Israel’s Central Elections Committee, Justice Noam Sohlberg, that there was no suspicion the results were invalid, the news site Ynet reported. The Shin Bet chief had pushed for a tougher inquiry, but investigators found no evidence of skewed results in Arab municipalities. Coalition talks continue ahead of the December 6 deadline.

briefs.title: Japan’s ruling bloc demands a bigger five-year defence budget
briefs.text: Lawmakers in Japan’s ruling coalition rejected a government plan to spend about 60 trillion yen on defence over the five years from 2027 and called for at least 70 trillion, Jiji Press reported. They argue that payments for equipment already bought in instalments, estimated by the defence ministry at 16.8 trillion yen, would eat into the budget. The government is revising its three main security documents by the end of the year.

oceania.summary: Australia’s parliament opens its last sitting week of the year with Labor tied with One Nation in a new poll and under fire over COP31, where Chris Bowen led the talks.

briefs.title: Newspoll puts One Nation level with Labor in Australia
briefs.text: A Newspoll published by The Australian on Sunday night put Labor and One Nation on 27 per cent each, with the Coalition on 22 and the Greens on 14. For the first time, opposition leader Angus Taylor led Anthony Albanese as preferred prime minister, by 42 to 41. Parliament began its final sitting week of the year on Monday with several government bills still needing support from the Greens or the Coalition.

briefs.title: Singapore’s prime minister arrives for annual talks with Australia
briefs.text: Lawrence Wong began a three-day visit to Australia on Monday for the eleventh annual Singapore–Australia leaders’ meeting in Canberra and Sydney, flying in on Singapore Airlines’ first service to the new Western Sydney International airport. He is also due to meet opposition leader Angus Taylor and New South Wales Premier Chris Minns.
